citations.quote: This paper introduces the Agile Mission Development Facility (AMDF), a concept for a new mission development platform at NASA Wallops that will develop a specific kind of Earth observing missions based on networks of small assets (CubeSats, UAVs and balloons) in a timeframe of weeks to months.

To achieve this reduced development time, the AMDF will use a new catalog-based and platform-based approach to mission design that emphasizes commonality at the subsystem or assembly level and the use of COTS components when possible. This will necessarily constrain the range of performance achievable by these missions, since only a few alternatives will be available for each subsystem. Only missions whose objectives can be achieved through a combination of the available modules will be considered.

The AMDF will maximize reuse of existing design, integration and testing software and hardware infrastructure at NASA Wallops as well as other NASA centers. All potentially relevant stakeholders, such as NASA Goddard, Headquarters, JPL, Ames, the Aerospace Corp., Applied Physics Lab, and universities with nanosatellite programs will be involved and considered in the AMDF development process.

This paper focuses on the description of the design aspects of the AMDF, as this is where most of the novelty lies. Integration, testing, launching and operations are only briefly discussed. A description of the system architecture of the AMDF is given using model-based systems engineering tools (SysML). An example application mission to measure ecological changes in the Jefferson and Washington National Forests is also discussed to illustrate the new kinds of missions that this facility could enable.
It currently takes months if not years to develop any kind of mission, which precludes missions especially designed to respond to events of interest and slows down technology infusion.

To describe the architecture of the AMDF, we follow the System Architecture process recommended by best practices, starting from the needs of the stakeholders and the concept of operations, continuing with a functional decomposition of the goals, an allocation of the functions to components, and the aggregation of these components into subsystems. While several architecture frameworks and methodologies exist [35], [36], [37], [38], [39], all of them coincide in the common set of steps with only minor differences.

Once the product platform is designed, the facility will be used as follows: the customer will provide an initial set of mission-specific requirements such as payload mass, power, volume and data throughput, control accuracy and slewing agility among others. An intelligent design tool featuring a database of modules (e.g., communications system, attitude control systems, electrical power systems) will then systematically explore the space of all possible mission configurations based on these modules. All valid configurations will be tested against the set of mission requirements and several options will be provided to the customer that optimize the trade-offs between all (potentially conflicting) requirements and cost in order to facilitate the final selection.

Note that a possible outcome of this step is that the desired missions cannot be achieved with the current platform and therefore it is recommended to use other more traditional NASA means to design the mission. If one or more acceptable designs exist, then the decision maker will choose one, and a point design will be conducted including detailed mass, power, data rate, pointing, and reliability budgets for all assets, mission analysis predictions including coverage, contact times between assets, and target revisit time statistics, a CAD model and a 3D prototype of all the assets if desired.

The main steps of the process are: 1. Identify the stakeholders, including customers, sponsors, suppliers, regulators, and other relevant organizations. 2. Identify the needs of each stakeholder, which may involve the exchange of money, products, services, information or influence among others. 3. Prioritize and group stakeholders as needed. Stakeholders with similar needs can be grouped together for the purpose of analysis and prioritization. 4. Characterize the needs of the stakeholders in terms of attributes such as intensity of the need, urgency, to what extent it can be fulfilled by other stakeholders, and so forth. 5. Prioritize the needs of the stakeholders, to get an idea of what are the most important outputs and value flows for the project.

The AMDF operations start with a set of meetings with the customer to define the concept of operations and high-level requirements of their Earth observation mission. After a Systems Requirement Review, the next step is to conduct a design tradespace exploration study looking at the space of all possible designs based on the AMDF product platform that satisfy the customer requirements - if any.

A description of a functional architecture must contain three high-level pieces of information: - A hierarchical decomposition of the system's primary function (a.k.a. the externally delivered function) into internal functions. - A description of the connectivity between functions, consisting of object (operand) flows and control flows. - A mapping between the system's goals and the system's functions, to show the traceability of intent.

Exploring the design space with the product platform (F2): This function consists in generating a large number of alternative designs based on the product platform, calculating their cost and performance, evaluating them against the customer requirements, and presenting the information to the user about the cost-effectiveness of different designs as well as the trade-offs between a handful of the most promising designs. The outcome of this function should be a conceptual design that is ready to go through a Mission Concept Review (MCR).

The outcome of this function should be a system design that is ready to go through a Preliminary Design Review (PDR).

Supporting detailed design (F4): This function consists in supporting the user in conducting a detailed design of all missions elements. While the need for detailed design is reduced by the fact that the assemblies are already designed in the product platform, there is still some detailed design work that needs to be done to ensure that a particular design is feasible.

Integration and testing (F5): The AMDF is also responsible for integrating and testing the system elements such as CubeSats and UAVs. This function decomposes into performing the traditional tests, namely: a) thermal vacuum test for all space assets; b) anechoic chamber tests for the antennas; c) vibration tests; d) electrical tests (continuity, isolation, voltage and currents for all electrical components); e) component and system-level functional tests for all electrical components (flatboard tests running flight and ground software). The outcome of this function should be a design that is ready to go through a Flight Readiness Review (FRR).

The primary functional flow is the control flow that determines the basic sequence of activities in the mission development process. The flow incorporates several key decision points that model the traditional design reviews.

From the standpoint of operand flows, the main operands are the design models and documents during the design activities and the system (and components) at various stages of integration as well as the procedures for integration, testing and operation of the system.

While it is not desirable to change the optimal components of the product platform at every mission, it is necessary to periodically check components for obsolescence and rerun the platform optimization algorithm with current technological and market assumptions to make sure that the platform is not too far from optimal.

The software platform, developed primarily by the Systems Engineering, Architecture and Knowledge (SEAK) Lab at Cornell University, consists of several hundreds of thousands of lines of code in Java, JESS and Python devoted to the automatic generation and evaluation of mission designs based on the product platform, as well as extensive decision support software such as evolutionary hyper-heuristic optimization algorithms, advanced visual analytics and advanced explanation facilities for enhanced human-computer interactions. citations.quote: The AMDF achieves very short development times without sacrificing too much of the custom design performance by leveraging the idea of product platforms and using advanced design optimization tools. These tools explore all possible combinations of designs based on a catalog of available modules in the platform and find the most affordable configuration that satisfies all mission requirements, or propose multiple missions at different points on the non-dominated cost-performance curve. This allows expediting the mission design process and also reduces the amount of testing necessary, since only a few combinations of modules are allowed, and all the modules have been thoroughly developed and tested for compatibility before.

While the paper has attempted to show that an AMDF concept as described could be valuable, the study presented in this paper is only a preliminary description of the concept for the purposes of discussion and does not constitute a complete feasibility analysis of the concept.
It is unclear that NASA customers would currently accept relatively high levels of risk or any loss in performance at all, even if the benefits in terms of cost and development time are important.

Implementing a commonality strategy presents challenges by itself. Two of the most common ones are divergence and managing through the so-called commonality gap. Divergence is a phenomenon by which the originally planned amount of commonality across products in the family decreases over time as the platform is implemented, due to a variety of reasons.

The commonality gap refers to the time that elapses between the moment where the investment for the development of the product platform is done and when the benefits of the commonality manifest themselves (presumably starting after the design of the nth variant). This time lapse can be of several months or even years, thus making it difficult for managers to navigate [47].
